transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-20 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Marcus (AstraHealth Head of ML), Priya (Eng Manager), Olivia (Infra)
Shared artifacts: Google Sheet - benchmark-results (drive.google.com/drive/fake-link), security pack (drive.google.com/drive/security-pack), benchmark logs (link in chat)

[00:00:05] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick agenda — review last week's benchmark, talk through the anomalies Marcus flagged, and decide next tests. We have Liam running through the numbers.
[00:00:22] Liam: Hey, yeah hi all. So I'm gonna share my screen — uh — the sheet that Samira linked. Quick note, some of the column headers were auto-transcribed by the tool so, excuse the weird names.
[00:00:35] Marcus: that's fine. quick context: last week we ran the baseline (CloudGen) and the Redwood setup with the same model family, same token length distribution, roughly 2k sample requests, and we saw differences. We wanted to understand why the p95 discrepancy was so large.
[00:00:50] Liam: Right. Summary first: median latency Redwood ~65ms, p95 ~120ms, p99 ~220ms under our test load. Baseline CloudGen median ~110ms, p95 ~310ms, p99 ~620ms. Throughput-wise we sustained ~420 rps on Redwood with small batching, baseline sustained ~260 rps before error/retry increase.
[00:01:10] Priya: those numbers look great on median and p95 but p99 seems still high for Redwood — 220ms is not bad but for our SLA we need <200 p99 ideally.
[00:01:22] Olivia: also curious about how repeatable those numbers are — are we using prefix caching? KV cache? We didn't see that in the baseline run.
[00:01:34] Liam: Great callouts. For the Redwood runs, we had prefix caching enabled at 80% hit rate in the simulation — realistic for your workload per the prompt set you sent. KV cache yes, we measured cache hit ratios in the sheet. For baseline runs, CloudGen's config didn't enable KV cache due to their managed endpoint limitations, which likely explains some of the tail behavior.
[00:01:58] Marcus: hmm ok. Could the difference be due to quantization or different kernel choices?
[00:02:05] Liam: There's a mix. We ran Redwood on a 16GB quantized variant (4-bit) for cost parity; baseline ran on their default 8-bit optimized path. In practice quantization reduces memory pressure and improves throughput, but sometimes you see p99 tail increases if KV eviction patterns are suboptimal. Also our runtime switches kernels per sequence length which helps medians.
[00:02:30] [00:02:30] Speaker 1 (auto): yeah so like um
[00:02:33] Samira: (laughs) ignore the auto voice. Back to the numbers — Liam, can you walk us through the CPU/GPU utilization graphs?
[00:02:40] Liam: Sure. On Redwood runs GPU util averaged 72%, spikes to low 90s during big batches. Baseline provider showed higher CUDA stall and more frequent context switches, util around 85% but with larger variance, which correlates with higher tail latencies.
[00:02:58] Priya: do you have per-request breakdown? We saw some outliers tied to very long prompts.
[00:03:05] Liam: Yup — there's a column with request length; the p99s are dominated by long prefix sequences and the synthetic long prompts we included. When we filter to typical 75th percentile length, Redwood p99 drops to ~160ms.
[00:03:20] Marcus: Ok that suggests maybe controlling prompt length or pre-truncation could be a mitigation. What's the tradeoff with quality when we do that?
[00:03:28] Liam: Slight drop on hallucination checks for extreme truncation; we ran automated evals — accuracy drop ~1.3% for aggressive truncation on few-shot prompts. We can share the eval set.
[00:03:40] Olivia: On the infra side — curious about VPC/private deployment. If we went private, how will that affect latency and throughput? We need consistent regional routing.
[00:03:50] Samira: Good Q. For Private (VPC) deployments we generally see similar latency once network egress is controlled — but initial setup adds a bit of overhead. Typical uplift 10–20ms network latency depending on partner cloud. For your region (us-west) should be lower. Also key management (KMS) integration happens at the control plane and doesn't add per-request overhead.
[00:04:12] Marcus: Are audit logs and SOC2 stuff available in the POC?
[00:04:16] Samira: Yes we shared the security pack in the chat — includes SOC 2 attestation, RBAC, SAML SSO options. For enterprise Private we can bring in HSM/KMS per your compliance team.
[00:04:28] [00:04:28] Speaker 2: mm hmm
[00:04:30] Liam: Back to tuning — we ran two additional runs this week: one with continuous batching at 50ms window, one with stricter 20ms. The 50ms window increased throughput to ~500 rps but added median latency ~+15ms. The 20ms window kept median low but throughput dropped to 340 rps. So there's a clear latency vs cost/throughput tradeoff.
[00:04:54] Priya: For our use case we need more consistent latency than absolute max throughput; so probably lower batching windows. Could caching help us keep throughput without increasing median?
[00:05:03] Liam: Yes, prefix/KV cache helps a lot. In a run where we had an 85% cache hit, effective token generation decreased ~38%, p95 dropped by ~45% in practice. The key is realistic hit patterns — your prompt reuse looked good in the sample set.
[00:05:20] Marcus: Can we reproduce CloudGen with caching off to be apples-to-apples?
[00:05:25] Liam: We tried. CloudGen's managed offering doesn't give low-level cache controls; so we ran their endpoint as-is. We also ran a control where we disabled caching on Redwood and the p95 moved closer to 230ms, still below baseline but gap narrowed.
[00:05:42] Samira: Important to note — the baseline runs also had higher retry rates under sustained load which inflated their p99 since retries re-enter the queue. We saw error rates bump at ~290 rps for CloudGen.
[00:05:55] Priya: Ok. Marcus — what's your timeline for a decision? Last we discussed end of August for pilot completion.
[00:06:03] Marcus: Correct. We want to lock performance feasibility by mid-August. Next few weeks we need the extra p99 tests and cost comparison.
[00:06:12] Liam: I'll run targeted p99 tests that isolate long-prefix behavior and also run a cold-cache vs warm-cache set. I'll push raw logs to the spreadsheet and a GCS bucket.
[00:06:22] Olivia: On infra day — we'd like to schedule an on-prem mimic run where we can validate VPC latency and E2E networking. What's the effort level to spin that up?
[00:06:33] Samira: We can do an infra day — two engineers from Redwood (SE + infra) and two from Astra. Expect 3–4 hours to get the private cluster mimic up and run a smoke benchmark. We'll need your network team to open ports and share a test subnet.
[00:06:49] Marcus: We can do that the week of 7/27.
[00:06:52] [00:06:52] Speaker 3: ok ok
[00:06:55] Liam: One more data point — cost parity. With quantized models and caching we estimate per-1M token cost at $18 on Redwood vs $28 on baseline (CloudGen) in their managed config. That's before reserved capacity discounts; we can provide committed pricing options.
[00:07:15] Priya: That gap is meaningful. What's included in that cost calc? GPU runtime, networking, caching overhead?
[00:07:21] Liam: It's GPU time, memory overhead, and our internal amortized infra — network egress costs are modeled separately. The sheet breaks it down per-token.
[00:07:29] Marcus: Any potential gotchas if we go quantized — is accuracy solid across our evals?
[00:07:35] Liam: In our evals quantized 4-bit shows negligible change for your primary tasks; on a few fine-grained NLU tasks there was minor drift but within tolerance. We'll give a side-by-side eval report.
[00:07:47] Samira: Alright let's capture the concrete next steps — Liam will run the p95/p99 with caching variations and share logs by Friday. Samira will share pricing and security docs by tomorrow. Marcus will provide traffic sample and confirm infra day for 7/27.
[00:08:05] Marcus: Sounds good. Quick question — you mentioned fallback policies earlier, how do rollouts look in Redwood? If we pin a model and then want to fallback to a cheaper variant, is that automatic?
[00:08:15] Samira: Yes — Redwood supports rollout policies, canary and automatic fallback to compatible variants if a region or capacity tier is unhealthy. We can demo that during infra day.
[00:08:25] Priya: Can we also get tracing hooks for per-request cost attribution?
[00:08:29] Liam: Yep we have token-level tracing and per-route dashboards in the console; we'll share a demo link.
[00:08:36] [00:08:36] Speaker 4: uh huh
[00:08:40] Samira: Any other risks we should call out?
[00:08:42] Marcus: Only the p99 target — need to see reproducible numbers. Also procurement wants clearer T&Cs around data retention.
[00:08:50] Samira: We'll include data retention language in the docs.
[00:08:54] Priya: can you also include an example SAML metadata for our IdP?
[00:08:58] Samira: Will do.
[00:09:00] Liam: I'll get started on the p99 isolation tests now and will post the logs. Expect raw latencies and kernel-level traces.
[00:09:08] Marcus: great, thanks.
[00:09:10] Samira: Ok everyone, thanks — recap and I'll send notes.
[00:09:15] Meeting end.

Notes about transcript: occasional auto-transcribed 'V-P-C' instead of VPC, 'K-V cash' for KV cache, and some speaker labels generic from the recorder.
